At 0.5 the wave grows by up to 12 % over 15 periods, so we recommend 0.1 or less. One error remains, namely an overprediction of the horizontal water velocity below the wave crest. All three solvers exhibit this error, which grows steadily with time. In Part II we trace this error to the implicit discretisation of the momentum convection term.

papers.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
papers.abstract: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

papers.title: GenerativeQC: A Generative, GPU-Accelerated Quantum Chemistry Program
papers.abstract: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that computes energies and analytic nuclear forces from Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT) to closed-shell density-fitted CCSD(T) and an MP2-assisted CCSD(T)/complete-basis-set (CBS) composite. Its scientific compiler translates symbolic equations into C++ and CUDA code and uses automatic differentiation to generate the derivative and response programs required for analytic forces. A native runtime executes these programs together with hand-written iterative solvers and integral routines. Across Direct and density-fitted HF and DFT benchmarks for eight methods on water clusters of up to 96 atoms, GenerativeQC is faster than GPU4PySCF in every tested case on both RTX 5090 and H100 GPUs. For correlated wave functions, compiler-generated derivative contractions and transpose Jacobian operators enable complete density-fitted CCSD(T) and CCSD(T)/CBS analytic forces on GPUs; a CCSD(T)/CBS energy-and-force calculation for heptane (23 atoms) takes 4.5 min on a single H100 GPU and 17 min on an RTX 5090.

papers.title: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate
papers.abstract: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

papers.title: Asymptotic probabilities in random Latin squares
papers.abstract: We introduce some new general techniques for studying asymptotic probabilities in random Latin squares. Using these techniques, we obtain an asymptotic formula for the probability that a given 'small' partial Latin square $H$ is present in a uniformly random $n\times n$ Latin square (as conjectured by Divoux-Kelly-Kennedy-Sidhu). As applications, we determine which configurations are likely to appear in random Latin squares (resolving a conjecture of Allsop-Morris), we determine the asymptotic distribution of the number of $3\times 3$ Latin subsquares in a uniformly random $n\times n$ Latin square (resolving conjectures of McKay-Wanless and Kwan-Sah-Sawhney), and we show that the first two rows of a random $n\times n$ Latin square are statistically indistinguishable from a random derangement (answering a conjecture of Cameron and Cavenagh-Greenhill-Wanless).

papers.title: Biases and Limits of AlphaFold Predictions for Non-Globular Proteins
papers.abstract: AlphaFold has transformed protein structure prediction, making structural models accessible across the life sciences. We explore experimentally validated cases of non-globular proteins to uncover where predictions diverge from biologically relevant structural states and how molecular context shapes these discrepancies, guiding a more informed interpretation of AlphaFold models.

papers.title: SCRiD: Spatial and Contextual References for Generalizable AI-Generated Video Detection
papers.abstract: Generalizable AI-generated video detection remains challenging because natural motion and content variations can resemble synthesis artifacts, making isolated video discrepancies unreliable indicators of authenticity. To address this challenge, we propose Spatial and Contextual Reference-informed Detection (SCRiD), a framework that interprets video variations through complementary spatial and contextual references. Specifically, we introduce Matched-Coordinate Residual Response (MCR) to characterize temporal residual associations under motion and coordinate references with matched subpixel sampling conditions. We further develop Real-Conditioned Score Adaptation (RCSA), which learns a content-conditioned denoising reference from authentic videos and probes its responses across multiple noise scales and quality views to guide feature adaptation. To integrate these complementary sources of evidence, we design Reversible Evidence Exchange (REE) to enable information exchange through reversible symplectic updates. We train SCRiD using synthetic videos from only 4 generators and evaluate it across 88 generator or task subsets spanning 6 benchmarks. Our method achieves average ACC and AP of 72.72% and 74.23%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.24 and 0.81 percentage points. Ablation and robustness experiments further validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and the stability of SCRiD under common post-processing operations.

papers.title: Semi-exact functors and the conjecture of Coulembier and Flake
papers.abstract: We introduce the notion of semi-exact functors between abelian categories, which are characterised by either preserving or breaking exactness of sequences. We prove semi-exact functors are always exact with respect to a canonically determined exact structure. For a symmetric tensor category $\mathscr{C}$, we define a support theory by considering all $\Bbbk$-linear symmetric monoidal, semi-exact functors $\mathscr{C}\to\operatorname{Ver}_{p^\infty}$ up to equivalence, and conjecture that it agrees with the Balmer spectrum of the stable category when $\mathscr{C}$ is finite. We prove a weak form of this conjecture and other results for Tannakian categories and in characteristic 0. Critical to the positive characteristic case is a functor constructed by Coulembier and Flake who were interested in higher Frobenius functors. We show that their construction, which relies on the theory of abelian envelopes, gives a natural source for semi-exact functors, and at least in the Tannakian setting gives all $\Bbbk$-linear, symmetric monoidal, semi-exact functors.

papers.title: Stabilized negative viscosity governs ocean jets before, during and after they leave the coast
papers.abstract: Eddies in rotating turbulence can feed the jets that spawn them, resulting in the negative viscosity phenomenon. Taken alone, a negative viscosity represents up-gradient eddy fluxes and is often referred to as "antifriction" or "antidiffusion". Mathematically, it leads to an ill-posed problem. In two-dimensional turbulence theory, this problem can be resolved by representing the transfer from small to large scales by a stabilized negative viscosity (SNV), in which a negative Laplacian viscosity is balanced by its positive biharmonic counterpart. In purely two-dimensional turbulence, by the Taylor identity, a negative viscosity is up-gradient transport of vorticity, which mixing cannot produce; on a slope, mixing of potential vorticity can mimic it, and we test for this. Using two years of wide-swath satellite altimetry (SWOT), we measure the eddy momentum flux across the five subtropical western boundary currents in each current's own frame. Along the continental slope the eddies act with a negative viscosity of order $-10^{3}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$, with the SNV structure resolved in the Gulf Stream and the Agulhas. At separation from the slope the sign reverses in all five currents, and the eddies brake the flow. Downstream, in the free jets, the negative viscosity returns on the cyclonic flank, strengthened to $-10^{4}$ m$^{2}$ s$^{-1}$. Separation is where the current leaves the strong topographic $\beta$ of the slope, the constraint that orders the eddy transfer. In an eddy-resolving reanalysis the SNV form holds across three ocean basins, with its shape parameter set by the deformation radius.

papers.title: When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers
papers.abstract: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

papers.title: Do VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

papers.title: Cyclic Self-Dual Codes over Prime-Square Rings and Unimodular Lattices
papers.abstract: We present an explicit construction of cyclic Euclidean self-dual codes over $\mathbb{Z}/p^{2}\mathbb{Z}$, where $p$ is an odd prime, and use Construction~A to obtain unimodular lattices with large minimum norms. The construction is based on reciprocal factorizations of $x^n-1$. We explicitly describe the associated residue and torsion codes and analyze the relationship between minimum Euclidean weights and lattice minimum norms. We construct a unimodular lattice of minimum norm~$4$ in dimension~$49$, unimodular lattices of minimum norm~$5$ in dimensions $53$, $55$, $58$, $59$, and~$61$, and extremal unimodular lattices of minimum norm~$6$ in dimensions $69$ and~$71$. Using shadow theory and harmonic theta series, we prove that extremal unimodular lattices do not exist in dimensions $59$ and~$61$. Together with the known upper bounds, these results establish the optimality of the constructed lattices in all eight dimensions. In particular, we determine the previously unknown optimal minimum norms of unimodular lattices in five dimensions: $53$, $55$, $61$, $69$, and~$71$. We further construct unimodular lattices whose minimum norms are exactly one below the corresponding extremal bounds in dimensions $62$, $63$, $65$, $67$, $70$, $89$, $91$, $92$, $93$, and~$94$.

papers.title: Multi-epoch imaging observations of the Galactic Center with NIRCam and MIRI
papers.abstract: The center of the Milky Way is the densest and most extreme environment in our Galaxy, its most active star forming region, and the only galaxy nucleus where we can resolve stars down to about a solar mass on the main sequence. The Galactic Center (GC) contains a nuclear stellar disk, a nuclear star cluster, and a supermassive black hole, all embedded within the so-called Central Molecular Zone, which showcases conditions of the interstellar medium that are typically found in high-redshift star-forming regions. The GC hosts the highest concentration of massive stars in the Milky Way and hosts a large concentration of rare objects, such as Wolf Rayet stars and X-ray binaries. The GC is therefore an astrophysical target of outstanding importance. A multi-epoch JWST program enables novel science including the lifetime of planet-forming disks, the search for intermediate mass black holes, direct measurements of the multi-scale gravitational potential, and a deep measurement of the star formation history. Multi-epoch imaging observations with JWST's NIRCam and MIRI instruments will go far beyond Roman WFI surveys in terms of depth and astrometric and photometric precision because of its $3\times$ better resolution, and it expands spectral coverage in narrow bands and mid-infrared wavelength coverage. The proposed observations would correspond to a Treasury Program of about 420\,h, distributed over three epochs spaced three to five years apart.

papers.title: Electrostatic and Quantum Transport Engineering of Multilayer Ferroelectric Tunnel Junctions for Improved TER and RA Trade off
papers.abstract: Ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) are promising for non-volatile memory and neuromorphic computing, but achieving a high tunnel electroresistance ratio (TER) with a low resistance-area (RA) product remains challenging. In this work, TiN/Hf$_{0.5}$Zr$_{0.5}$O$_2$ (HZO)-based FTJs containing zero to three TiO$_2$ and IGZO-based quantum wells (QWs) are analyzed using the Miller ferroelectric (FE) polarization model integrated with the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism to examine the effects of QW material and thickness on polarization and transport. TiO$_2$-based structures exhibit higher polarization and TER than IGZO-based structures. At a read bias of 0.1 V, the uniform TiO$_2$ double-QW structure, with 1-nm-thick QW and insulating layer (IL) layers, gives a TER of $2.71\times10^{10}\%$ and an RA product of $5\times10^4~\Omega\cdot\text{cm}^2$, compared with $5.95\times10^7\%$ and $2\times10^5~\Omega\cdot\text{cm}^2$, respectively, for IGZO. Both uniform and non-uniform TiO$_2$ double-QW structures exhibit resonant tunneling (RT) and negative differential resistance (NDR) associated with QW-confined states. Increasing the first QW thickness to 1.38 nm, while keeping the second QW and both IL layers at 1 nm, shifts the confined-state energies and modifies resonant transport. The selected non-uniform structure achieves a TER of $2.95\times10^{11}\%$ and an RA product of $1.25\times10^3~\Omega\cdot\text{cm}^2$ at a read bias of 0.1 V. Elastic scattering changes the amplitude and width of QW resonant-transmission peaks, with a stronger effect on the low resistance state (LRS) than on the high resistance state (HRS). These results show that QW material and thickness optimization can improve the TER--RA trade-off, while electrode screening and elastic scattering further influence polarization-dependent transport in multilayer FTJs.

papers.title: RoughCut-Bench: A Benchmark for Automatic Video Rough-Cut with Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.

papers.title: Polarized positron generation via laser-engineered quasistatic magnetic fields in a spatially extended herringbone target
papers.abstract: Polarized positron sources are of interest for precision studies of spin-dependent interactions and future high-energy colliders, yet their laser-driven realization remains challenging because of demanding laser or beam requirements. Here, we propose a target-engineered scheme for generating polarized positrons using a 3.4-PW single-color laser pulse and an initially unpolarized 10-GeV electron beam. Three-dimensional spin-resolved quantum electrodynamics particle-in-cell simulations show that laser-driven return currents in a herringbone target generate spatially extended quasistatic magnetic fields exceeding $\simeq 10^6$ T, with opposite polarities and a duration exceeding 100 fs. These fields correlate positron spin polarization with deflection direction, enabling angular selection of two oppositely polarized positron populations with polarization magnitudes of 63\% and a combined yield of approximately 0.007 positrons per incident electron, compared with a total yield of 0.029. Our results demonstrate a route toward highly polarized positron generation under laser conditions accessible to existing petawatt-class facilities, without requiring frequency-converted ultraintense fields or prepolarized incident beams.

papers.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
papers.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

papers.title: On pluriclosed torsion-critical Hermitian metrics
papers.abstract: In our previous work, we studied the squared $L^2$-norm functionals $\mathcal G$ of Gauduchon's torsion $1$-form and $\mathcal F$ of the Chern torsion over the space of all Hermitian metrics with unit volume on a compact complex manifold. We introduced torsion-critical metrics as critical points of $\mathcal F$. In this paper, We prove that a pluriclosed and astheno-K\"ahler metric is torsion-critical if and only if it is K\"ahler. In particular, every compact pluriclosed torsion-critical Hermitian threefold is K\"ahler. We also give explicit examples and derive geometric consequences under additional curvature assumptions.

papers.title: Circuit spectra for binary matroids
papers.abstract: The circuit spectrum of a matroid is defined to be the set of circuit sizes. The circuit $e$-spectrum of a matroid is the set of circuit sizes of the matroid containing the element $e$. The circuit spectrum problem is an important problem. Erd\H{o}s (1992) conjectured that every connected graph $G$ with girth $g$ and average degree $d$ has a cycle spectrum of size at least $\Omega(d^{\lfloor (g-1)/2 \rfloor})$. Sudakov and Verstra\"{e}te (2008) proved the full conjecture of Erd\H{o}s in a stronger form. It is natural to consider the size of the circuit spectra of binary matroids. Murty (1971) characterized all connected binary matroids with circuit spectra of size one. Lemos et al. (2011) characterized the connected binary matroids with circuit spectra of size two, where the largest size is odd. For general binary matroids, it is still an open question to find a lower bound for the size of the circuit spectra. In this paper, we give best-possible such lower bounds for connected binary matroids that do not contain both the Fano matroid and its dual as minors. Let $M$ be a simple connected binary matroid that does not have both the Fano matroid and its dual as a minor, and $d\geq 3$ be the minimum cocircuit size of $M$. We prove that (1) for each element $e$ of $M$, the circuit $e$-spectrum of $M$ must have size at least $d-2$. This bound is best possible. (2) The circuit spectrum of $M$ must have size at least $d-1$, unless $M\cong F_7,F_7^*,R_{10}$. In exceptional cases, the spectrum of $M$ has size equal to $d-2$.

papers.title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
papers.abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

papers.title: Autoregressive View Model
papers.abstract: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.

papers.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

papers.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
papers.abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

papers.title: The Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture fails over the reals
papers.abstract: In 1986 Bapat and Sunder asked whether $\operatorname{per}(A)$ is the largest eigenvalue of $F_A=[a_{i,j}\operatorname{per}(A(i,j))]$ for every positive semidefinite Hermitian $A$, where $A(i,j)$ deletes row $i$ and column $j$. Drury disproved this over the complex field in 2018 and conjectured that the property holds for real positive semidefinite matrices. We disprove Drury's conjecture with a rank-$4$, $32\times32$ integer Gram matrix and an integer vector whose Rayleigh quotient exceeds $\operatorname{per}(A)$; verification uses integer arithmetic. Together, the two counterexamples resolve the Bapat-Sunder eigenvalue conjecture negatively over both fields. Counterexamples exist of every order $n\ge32$. As an application to quantum optics, the violation yields a $36$-mode orthogonal interferometer and a direction of relative arrival-time delays among $32$ photons with identical-variance Gaussian wave packets along which every sufficiently small nonzero delay increases the probability that all photons are detected within four designated output modes.

papers.title: EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
papers.abstract: Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.

papers.title: Memory kernel and closure for systems driven by intermittent forcing with power-law waiting times
papers.abstract: Many systems are driven by an intermittent forcing that takes on a random value for a random time interval. For such renewal step noise, the master equation for the driven variable has a memory kernel whose coefficients are the totally time-ordered cumulants, or $G$-cumulants, of the noise. In the case of Poisson switching, these correspond to the Boolean cumulants of the jump distribution, and the kernel can be summed exactly. We derive an exact decomposition of these coefficients for any waiting-time distribution with independent amplitudes and durations, which separates the jump statistics from the renewal statistics. For power-law waiting-time densities, $\psi(\theta)\propto\theta^{-\mu}$ with $\mu>2$ (finite mean), a long time interval is most likely covered by a single epoch, and we prove that, as a result, the coefficients cross over at long lags, at all orders, from the Boolean cumulants to the ordinary moments of the jump law. The long-lag kernel thus becomes a superposition of the kernels of the frozen deterministic flows, weighted by $\xi^2p(\xi)$, and the corresponding master equation follows in closed form. For $2<\mu<3$, where the noise correlation time is infinite, the second-order closure retains a finite error even for slow dynamics, whereas the frozen-flow master equation yields the exact stationary mean in that limit. The telegraph process is the only renewal step noise for which the second-order closure is exact. An exactly solvable model with correlated additive and multiplicative noise confirms these predictions.

papers.title: Event-Based Person Detection for Maritime UAV Search
papers.abstract: Maritime search and rescue requires locating people in the water quickly, motivating the use of UAVs to survey the search area. During flight, camera motion and the longer exposures used in low light can blur small targets and hinder person detection. Event cameras record brightness changes as they occur, reducing the motion blur associated with longer exposure times. We investigate their use for maritime person detection by generating synthetic events using the v2e event simulator from public MOBDrone rescue videos and retaining the existing annotations. We compare the recurrent vision transformer model RVT-T with YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images. On 843 test samples from held-out recordings, RVT-T achieves 15.63% person AP50:95, compared with 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18 under 100 ms synthetic exposure. Increasing exposure times from 50 to 200 ms progressively reduces frame-based detection accuracy, widening the gap to the event model. To evaluate the feasibility of on-board processing, we deploy our detector on a Jetson Orin Nano platform. The RVT-T model retains its accuracy and requires approximately 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample, allowing real-time processing on the UAV.

papers.title: Banchoff Curvature and Realisation Moduli of Piecewise-Affine Arrangement Immersions
papers.abstract: We compute the curvature concentrated on the flats of a piecewise-affine immersion of $\mathbb{R}^D$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$ creased along an affine hyperplane arrangement, and parametrise the immersions sharing its chamber metrics. Suppose every transverse crease cone is embedded (the positive-path-rank condition). Then the Gauss-Bonnet-Chern density of any convex coordinate-wise smoothing that is affine outside a compact transition zone reduces, on each transverse slice, to a Hafnian. This Hafnian integrates to Banchoff's critical-point curvature on each even-codimension flat. The curvature coincides with the Cheeger-M\"uller-Schrader density and equals an alternating sum of Gaussian orthant probabilities determined by Schur complements of the incident chamber metrics. In even dimension, under mild non-degeneracy, total vertex curvature equals the recession curvature at infinity and is unchanged when the walls are translated, even across multi-wall collisions. Under generic codimension-two intersections, realisations with prescribed chamber metrics form a compact rank-constrained spectrahedron of generic local dimension $\max(0,H-r(r+1)/2)$, where $r = \max(0,D+H-n)$. At minimal target dimension the given immersion is the unique realisation preserving orientation across each single wall, and a positive semidefinite stress matrix certifies universal rigidity.

papers.title: KL-Guided Support Selection and Subspace Cubic Newton Methods for Sparse Optimization
papers.abstract: We study sparse composite optimization with a smooth loss and a possibly nonconvex, nonsmooth regularizer. The objective is locally smooth on each fixed support. Our method combines full-space proximal-gradient steps with inexact cubic-regularized Newton steps on a subspace selected by thresholding. If the iterates are bounded and the objective satisfies the Kurdyka--\L ojasiewicz (KL) property, the entire sequence converges to a first-order stationary point. A threshold based on the KL exponent ensures that the selected coordinate set coincides with the support of the limit after finitely many iterations, without requiring a nondegeneracy assumption. We also provide a residual-based threshold when such an exponent exists and its value is unknown. Under an additional continuity assumption on the restricted Hessian, the line search eventually accepts full cubic steps. With bounded cubic regularization parameters and damping parameters chosen to meet the target tolerances, we bound the number of outer iterations needed to reach restricted approximate second-order stationarity after support identification and entry into the full-step regime. We conduct numerical experiments in two settings: when the KL exponent is known and when it is unknown. In the former case, we use a degenerate problem to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. In the latter case, we compare the proposed method and its adaptive variant with existing solvers on sparse recovery and logistic regression problems.

papers.title: Commutants of diagonal operators
papers.abstract: The aim of this paper is devoted to the profound and comprehensive characterization when diagonal operators having the minimal, tiny or double commutant property on a separable Hilbert space, in terms of the topological and geometric properties of their spectra.

papers.title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
papers.abstract: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

papers.title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
papers.abstract: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBench drops by only 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. PCRG shortens the sequence rather than changing how attention is computed or which steps are run, so it also stacks on step caching and sparse attention. On V2V-Bench it reaches 1.86x with TeaCache, 1.82x with Spark at nearly unchanged fidelity and 2.15x with Veda.

papers.title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
papers.abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

papers.title: From Relevance to Utility: Rubric Alignment in Yuanbao Search
papers.abstract: Agentic search demands that a search engine move beyond per document relevance ranking to assemble document sets optimized for downstream LLM reasoning. Prior work addresses this either by improving individual pipeline stages in isolation or by applying RL based selection on top of relevance trained upstream modules, leaving the full stack unaligned to utility for reasoning. We propose rubric aligned search, a framework that unifies the traditional search pipeline under a single supervision surface. For each query, we derive a rubric from coarse to fine, specifying weighted positive criteria that the document set must satisfy and negative criteria that it must avoid. From this rubric we derive two training signals. First, a lightweight labeler distills rubric grounded judgments into per document utility labels, which supervise a contrastive dual encoder for retrieval and a multi task ranker trained with four rubric aligned scoring heads. Second, a rubric conditioned evaluator produces a set level reward that drives a dual branch RL selector, combining GRPO with best rollout distillation to resolve credit assignment in subset optimization. Deployed in Yuanbao Search, the pipeline improves end to end answer quality by 8.52% over the online production baseline.

papers.title: Equivariant Flow Matching on Homogeneous Spaces
papers.abstract: Flow matching enables the training of networks that can flow samples from an initial to a target distribution. The network is regressed against simple vector fields that are conditioned on end points in the target distribution. In the Euclidean case, these conditional vector fields induce flows along straight lines. Various generalisations have been proposed to perform flow matching on spaces where straight lines are not well-defined, such as Riemannian manifolds and Lie groups. Riemannian flow matching applies to many domains, but typically requires expensive simulation, while flow matching on Lie groups is simulation-free but only works on Lie groups. In this work, we develop equivariant flow matching on homogeneous spaces, which generalises flow matching on Lie groups, while remaining simulation-free. We also derive all generators connecting pairs of position-orientations and perform a similar derivation for event-velocity space, the Lorentzian analogue of position-orientation space, so that we can perform flow matching on these spaces.

papers.title: SRED: Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation Across Magnifications in Whole-Slide Imaging
papers.abstract: In computational pathology, high-magnification whole-slide image analysis preserves tissue detail but requires encoding many patches, whereas lower magnification reduces computation by covering a higher field of view per patch while sacrificing detail. Existing cross-magnification distillation matches features that often encode detail unreachable by low-magnification input, sometimes requiring slide-level labels that limit scalability. To address those issues, we introduce Sparse Regional Evidence Distillation (SRED), which transfers regional event occurrences that encode reachable high-level interactions between details without slide-level labels. We use a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to learn an event dictionary from 20x teacher features. Logical OR pooling records whether each event is detected in any spatially aligned patch, retaining both localized and shared evidence within the corresponding 5x region. A pretrained 5x encoder is fine-tuned to predict these regional targets without slide-level labels. Visual analysis identifies dictionary components responsive to recognizable histological patterns, supporting target interpretation. Compared with native 5x features, SRED improves average macro-F1 by 1.1 points across seven classification and grading cohorts and average C-index by 1.7 points across five survival cohorts. Runtime matches native 5x, with an average 11.58x speedup over 20x.

papers.title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Alongside memory storage and retrieval, a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems is how the agent should act when stored memories conflict with an evolving world. Facts often go stale without explicit deletion, so the conflict surfaces before the store is refreshed: delayed feedback shows that acting on one outdated record hurt, but not whether suppression should stay on that fact (a local policy) or extend to other stored facts (a global policy). Existing systems hard-code one of these scopes at design time. We formulate this online choice, under hidden validity and delayed feedback, as memory conflict governance, and propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight router that keeps both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them without retraining the LLM. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor, by off-path paired comparison or by inverse-propensity estimation from the executed action alone. A Local Advisor tracks only the queried fact, a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across the store, and an asymmetric Meta Governor follows Local by default, switching to Global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. We prove that using delayed outcomes escapes the prompt-only regret floor, that neither fixed scope suffices alone, and that this margin gate switches within bounded time. On LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, delays $\tau \in [1, 96]$, and sparse or bandit feedback, with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed scope in all 30 held-out settings, by 5.2-7.3 points on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, while cutting harmful stale-memory use at microsecond overhead.

papers.title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Fracture in Anisotropic Media
papers.abstract: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

papers.title: A Forensic Analysis of Metadata and Information Leakage in Swedish Public Documents
papers.abstract: This study investigates metadata and structural content leakage in publicly available PDF documents from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities. Using an automated collection pipeline and ExifTool-based extraction, 2,876 documents were analyzed and classified using an R0-R3 risk taxonomy. Results reveal that 48.4% of documents exhibit significant metadata exposure (R2 or R3), with significant variation across institutional tiers (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis across three legislative periods reveals a statistically significant reduction in metadata exposure between the baseline and post-enactment periods, yet 44.9% of documents published after the enactment of the Swedish Cybers\"akerhetslagen continue to leak sensitive metadata. Furthermore, 41.6% of documents contain incremental update layers; forensic analysis recovered verifiable text alterations, including deleted personal data and internal identifiers, from 228 of these cases. These findings highlight persistent regulatory lag and a systemic reliance on default, unsanitized document publication workflows within the Swedish public sector.

papers.title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection
papers.abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

papers.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
papers.abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

papers.title: All-Genus 2D $\mathcal{N}=1$ Superconformal Blocks
papers.abstract: We develop a numerical algorithm for two dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal blocks at arbitrary genera, in arbitrary plumbing channels, and for arbitrary spin structures. The algorithm utilizes two commuting copies of Virasoro subalgebras of the direct sum of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal algebra with an auxiliary free fermion algebra, which allows us to reduce the $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal blocks to Virasoro conformal blocks.

papers.title: Constraints on the volume enclosed by Fermi surfaces
papers.abstract: A fundamental property of a Fermi liquid (FL) is that the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by $\rho$, the total density of electrons. In a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*), the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by the same expression after $\rho$ has been shifted by a quantized amount, most commonly to $\rho -1$ (we assume spin rotation invariance, for simplicity). The FL* shift is related to the quantized symmetry fractionalization data of a quantum spin liquid, whose fractionalized spinon excitations are present alongside the Fermi surface quasiparticles. In this review article, we establish the FL* Fermi volume by generalizing the original Luttinger proof for FL to parton gauge theories of the quantum spin liquid and FL*. We also discuss Oshikawa's flux insertion arguments for FL, and their extension to FL*, including a discussion of gapless spin liquids.

papers.title: Quantum $K$-theoretic Whitney relation for Lagrangian Grassmannian
papers.abstract: We give a quantum $K$-theoretic analogue of the Whitney relation for the torus-equivariant $K$-ring of the Lagrangian Grassmannian. As a consequence, we give a presentation of the torus-equivariant quantum $K$-ring of the Lagrangian Grassmannian. The strategy for obtaining such relations is to use the quantum $K$-theoretic Whitney relation for the full-flag manifold in type $C$ established by the author and Kato's pushforward map from the quantum $K$-ring of the full-flag manifold to that of the partial flag manifold. Then the Nakayama-type argument established by Gu et al., together with the classical Whitney presentation for the torus-equivariant $K$-ring of the Lagrangian Grassmannian, gives a proof of such a presentation.

papers.title: A Scalable Decentralized Event-Triggered Topology-Switching Protocol for Verifiable Safe Control in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: This paper develops a decentralized event-triggered topology-switching protocol that allows agents to disconnect from the communication network while preserving state safety and excluding Zeno behavior. We establish a robust barrier function condition that guarantees safety as long as the estimation error remains within a prescribed threshold. Each agent uses locally computable certificates to determine when to connect and disconnect from the network. The certificate construction improves scalability by reducing the complexity of topology-dependent computations from $O(2^N)$ to $O(N)$, where $N$ is the number of agents. We formally prove that the protocol ensures the estimation error does not exceed the prescribed threshold and is non-Zeno. An alternating method computes an error-weighting matrix and a quadratic barrier function that guarantee safety under the proposed protocol. Finally, we evaluate the protocol on four interconnected microgrids. Compared with maintaining network connectivity at all times, the protocol reduces the time agents remain connected while keeping phase and frequency within their safe operating region.

papers.title: Synthetic Doubt and the Integrity of Digital Proof before the International Criminal Court
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence complicates evidentiary assessment at the International Criminal Court by enabling fabricated audiovisual material and making authentic digital evidence easier to dismiss as fake. This article calls the latter problem synthetic doubt: an objection alleging that a digital item may be AI-generated or AI-manipulated. Existing scholarship addresses digital evidence, open-source investigations and deepfakes in the ICC context. Yet the question of when synthetic doubt should trigger enhanced reliability review under the Rome Statute, without displacing the prosecution's burden under article 66 or compromising article 67 fair-trial rights, remains underdeveloped. The article proposes a three-stage framework: a baseline authenticity and provenance showing by the proponent; a case-specific articulation threshold for the objector; and proportionate reliability review by the Chamber under articles 64 and 69(4). The framework treats AI-related provenance information and synthetic-media detector outputs as contextual rather than dispositive.

papers.title: A counterexample to the soundness of the Flowering IOPP for codes on graphs
papers.abstract: The Flowering protocol of Delavenne, Medevielle and Roussel (ISIT 2025, arXiv:2501.14337) and its generalization by Delavenne and Lallemand (CANS 2025, arXiv:2508.10510) are Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (IOPPs) for codes on graphs with Reed-Solomon local codes. Similarly to FRI for Reed-Solomon codes, the graph is recursively cut into isomorphic subgraphs and the word is folded along the cuts. We show that the soundness claims of both papers are false. The commit soundness proofs identify the vertex distance of a word to the code with the fraction of its unsatisfied local constraints, while only one inequality holds, in the wrong direction. We furthermore give an explicit counterexample.

papers.title: Equivariant geometry of quadrics blown-up along a twisted quartic
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be the blow-up of a smooth quadric threefold along a twisted quartic, and let $G\subset\operatorname{Aut}(X)$ be a finite subgroup such that $\mathrm{Pic}^G(X)$ has rank one. We prove that $X$ is $G$-birationally superrigid if and only if $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_2$. The action of $G$ on $X$ is linearisable if and only if it is projectively linearisable, and this holds precisely when $G$ contains no subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_2^3$.

papers.title: WiTac: Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.abstract: Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts. Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.

papers.title: Renewable Estimation for Generalized Nonparametric Regression with Dynamic Spline Bases and Likelihood Pullback
papers.abstract: A fixed spline space may limit approximation accuracy in generalized nonparametric regression with streaming data. We propose a renewable penalized-likelihood method for generalized nonparametric regression with canonical exponential-family responses. Our method combines dynamic cubic-spline refinement with Gram-metric pullback of historical score and curvature summaries. The pullback preserves the retained historical likelihood quadratic on the embedded previous spline space, while incoming data update the fit and its summaries. Under regularity and algorithmic conditions, including a growing startup and an uncapped refinement regime, we establish $L^2$-consistency at rate $O_p(N^{-2/5})$ for a fixed target in $H^2[0,1]$ and a smaller-order energy-norm discrepancy from a matched offline estimator. Simulations and applications to the Voice and Catalina datasets show that dynamic bases improve estimation when the initial representation is restrictive, with additional gains from pullback. A preliminary computational comparison also shows lower computational and storage costs than the offline methods.

papers.title: Non-Hermitian edge accretion
papers.abstract: Under the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), it is generally taken for granted that the open boundary condition (OBC) spectrum is encircled by the periodic boundary condition (PBC) spectrum. Intuitively, this is because boundaries tend to block the directed NHSE amplification, thereby suppressing $\operatorname{Im}(E)$. In this work, we analytically and numerically demonstrate how this conventional scenario can be dramatically violated: In a phenomenon which we term non-Hermitian edge accretion (NHEA), strongly coupled competing NHSE channels conspire to amplify a state whenever it bounces off an edge, instead of attenuating it. This unexpected behavior arises from underappreciated consequences of non-Bloch eigenspinor orthogonality, which control the reflection coefficients as well as the balance between propagating and evanescent waves. Operating in the strongly coupled regime, NHEA is fundamentally distinct from conventional critical NHSE scaling, which is characterized by amplification feedback generated in the bulk, not the edges. Requiring only strongly coupled antagonistic NHSE chains with suitable mode orthogonality, the NHEA is platform-agnostic, and can be identified through periodically growing edge bounces in generic non-Hermitian metamaterials and quantum simulators.

papers.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

papers.title: The monogenicity of $\boldsymbol{x^n+c\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}a^{n-j-1}x^j}$
papers.abstract: We say that a monic polynomial $f(x)\in {\mathbb Z}[x]$ is {\em monogenic} if $f(x)$ is irreducible over ${\mathbb Q}$ and $\{1,\theta,\theta^2,\ldots,\theta^{{\rm deg}(f)-1}\}$ is a basis for the ring of integers of ${\mathbb Q}(\theta)$, where $f(\theta)=0$. Let $n,a,c\in {\mathbb Z}$ with $n\ge 3$, and suppose that \[{\mathcal F}_{n,a,c}(x):=x^n+cx^{n-1}+acx^{n-2}+a^2cx^{n-3}+\cdots +a^{n-2}cx+a^{n-1}c\] is irreducible over ${\mathbb Q}$. Recently, Jakhar, Kalwaniya and Yadav have given necessary and sufficient conditions for the monogenicity of ${\mathcal F}_{n,a,c}(x)$, under the assumption that all prime divisors of the discriminant of ${\mathcal F}_{n,a,c}(x)$ not dividing $ac$ also do not divide $n+1$. In this note, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the monogenicity of ${\mathcal F}_{n,a,c}(x)$ without this restriction.

papers.title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
papers.abstract: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, compute futures are listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. The contracts on CME and ICE reference published short-dated rental rates, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.4%.

papers.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
papers.abstract: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. In five-task sequences with slow forgetting, the stored bracket outperforms the EWC penalty on MNIST and CIFAR-10 features (by 0.16-0.17) and ties it on Fashion-MNIST; it fades as summaries age on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, where a Taylor estimate from the same summary holds up better. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition, provided the summary is kept fresh.

papers.title: CleanRoute: Reconciling DRC Compliance, Post-Layout Performance, and Routing Efficiency in Analog Routing
papers.abstract: Automated analog routing remains a long-standing challenge because design-rule checking (DRC) compliance, post-layout performance preservation, and runtime reduction are difficult to achieve together. Existing analog routers struggle to meet all three objectives due to limited design-rule coverage, insufficient control over topology-induced mismatch, or trade-offs between DRC violations and runtime on uniform routing grids. In this paper, we introduce CleanRoute, an analog router that reconciles these three targets. Hierarchical rule enforcement assigns DRC checks and repairs to stages where the required geometry is complete, covering rules both between separate metal and where metal joins. IR-drop isolation constructs supply trees from current-mirror relationships and device currents to reduce topology-induced mismatch that geometric matching cannot eliminate and voltage drops along high-current paths. A flush-line grid adds net-specific lines aligned with device-metal edges to a coarse routing grid, providing DRC-compliant connections without uniform refinement. Experiments on ten operational transconductance amplifiers (OTAs) in a commercial 40nm process show that CleanRoute produces DRC-clean and functional layouts that pass layout versus schematic (LVS) checking on all benchmarks, with the strongest overall performance preservation and a median routing runtime of 8.82s, whereas the baselines produce no DRC-clean layouts.

papers.title: Spectral Moments of the Projected Hubbard Configuration Graph: Connectivity, Exchange, and Virtual Doublons
papers.abstract: At strong repulsion, the lowest band of $n$ lattice fermions is the spectrum of the hopping projected onto states without double occupancy, $H_\infty=P_0H_tP_0$. We study its moments on the square lattice and, where possible, any finite graph. (1) For spin-independent Hermitian hopping (no on-site terms) on $N\geq2$ sites, $\mu_2=\frac{n(N-n)}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}|t_{ij}|^2$ for any spin composition. (2) On any finite graph, $\mu_4$ is exactly linear in the same-spin pair count $P_{\rm same}$ (four hops move at most three particles). For uniform hopping on a simple graph with $N\geq4$, $\mu_4=A+\alpha P_{\rm same}$ in closed form: the slope $\alpha=-8C_4(N-n)(8N-11n-2)/[N(N-1)(N-2)(N-3)]$ is set by the number $C_4$ of 4-cycles, the intercept, via hard-core bosons, by edge, edge-pair and 4-cycle counts. With arbitrary Peierls phases, $\mu_4$ is a spin-independent baseline plus a coefficient times $\sum_C\cos\Theta_C$ over 4-cycle Wilson phases. (3) At finite $U$, the second-order Schrieffer-Wolff correction is Hilbert-Schmidt orthogonal to $H_\infty$ on every triangle-free graph, so the band variance has no $1/U$ term; its $U^{-2}$ coefficient is negative at the low fillings computed. (4) Exchange loops carry the ordinary charge-$e$ harmonic, $\alpha\cos\Phi_\square$ on $L\times L$ tori, $L\neq4$, while the doublon hopping acquires a doubled phase, $t_de^{2iA_{ij}}$: the second-order single-doublon Hamiltonian is exactly $\pi$-periodic ($h/2e$) under a boundary twist, and the exact two-electron U-band follows up to $O((2\lambda)^L/U^{L-1})$. Result (1), the closed form in (2) without phases, the orthogonality in (3) and the doubled phase are machine-checked in Lean 4. Repulsive binding and the pair charge $2e$ are known; new are the exact moments and the derivation of the doubled phase. We make no claim about many-pair phase stiffness, off-diagonal long-range order or superconductivity.

papers.title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
papers.abstract: Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is not distinguishable in double-blind evaluation by either humans (8/16) or a calibrated LLM judge (9/16). A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; pilots 22/24 and 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swap, disagreement counted as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 (tie=0.5; bootstrap CI [0.708, 0.938]; hard-agree 0.900 [0.699, 0.972]), repetition 0.114 to 0.000, MMLU within noise. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain.
